newsitem.title: USA: New U.S. meat inspection starts.
newsitem.headline: New U.S. meat inspection starts.

text.p: The first phase of revolutionary new meat inspection rules, which require U.S. slaughter plants to test carcasses for the bacterium E. coli, went into effect Monday.
Meat plants are also required to have written rules on how they will make sure their animal slaughter and processing areas are properly sanitized.

In July, President Clinton announced a major overhaul to make meat and poultry inspection safer. The new rules mandate that slaughter and processing plants introduce over the next three years scientific testing for sickness-causing bacteria.

In his weekly radio address Saturday, Clinton proposed spending $43 million to track food-borne illnesses more aggressively and earmarked $8.5 million to help enforce the new meat and poultry inspection regulations.

Goverment inspectors previously relied on sight and smell to certify meat and poultry was safe to eat, a system little changed since Upton Sinclair's expose on the Chicago stockyards, "The Jungle," led to the enactment the Federal Meat Inspection Act in 1907.

The new test for generic E. coli, a bacterium found in the intestines of animals, will be used as a marker of fecal contamination in meat. Feces that spills onto meat when the intestines are removed after slaughter is a major source of contamination by disease-causing bacteria.
Generic E. coli is not harmful, unlike the virulent strain of the bacterium, 0157:H7, which killed four children in the Northwest in 1993 after they ate undercooked contaminated hamburgers.
Sara Lilygren, spokeswoman for the American Meat Institute, said the industry was ready for the new rules and noted that many companies already use the techniques.
"The beauty of this is that there is really going to be uniform use of very good sanitation and micro-testing processes throughout the industry," she said.

The next wave of meat inspection changes will occur this summer when the Agriculture Department will begin testing raw meat and poultry at slaughter plants for salmonella, the biggest food-borne killer.
The department estimates five million people become ill and more than 4,000 die each year because of contaminated meat and poultry products.
